But the high places were not taken away--</hi>The popular fondness for the private and disorderly rites performed in the groves and recesses of hills was so inveterate that even the most powerful monarchs had been unable to accomplish their suppression; no wonder that in the early reign of a young king, and after the gross irregularities that had been allowed during the maladministration of Athaliah, the difficulty of putting an end to the superstitions associated with "the high places" was greatly increased. <div eID="gen4897" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3471"/><div sID="gen4899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3471"/><hi type="bold">7-10. Why repair ye not the breaches of the house?--</hi>This mode of collection not proving so productive as was expected (the dilatoriness of the priests was the chief cause of the failure), a new arrangement was proposed. A chest was placed by the high priest at the entrance into the temple, into which the money given by the people for the repairs of the temple was to be put by the Levites who kept the door. The object of this chest was to make a separation between the money to be raised for the building from the other moneys destined for the general use of the priests, in the hope that the people would be more liberal in their contributions when it was known that their offerings would be devoted to the special purpose of making the necessary repairs. The duty of attending to this work was no longer to devolve on the priests, but to be undertaken by the king. <div eID="gen4899" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3472"/><div sID="gen4900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3472"/><hi type="bold">11-12. they gave the money, being told, into the hands of them that did the work--</hi>The king sent his secretary along with an agent of the high priest to count the money in the chest from time to time (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.11">2Ch 24:11</reference>), and deliver the amount to the overseers of the building, who paid the workmen and purchased all necessary materials. The custom of putting sums of certain amount in bags, which are labelled and sealed by a proper officer, is a common way of using the currency in Turkey and other Eastern countries. <div eID="gen4900" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3473"/><div sID="gen4901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3473"/><hi type="bold">13-16. Howbeit there were not made ... bowls, &c.--</hi>When the repairs of the temple had been completed, the surplus was appropriated to the purchase of the temple furniture. The integrity of the overseers of the work being undoubted, no account was exacted of the way in which they applied the money given to them, while other moneys levied at the temple were left to the disposal of the priests as the law directed (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.16">Le 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.5.8">Nu 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen4901" type="x-p"/>
